aspects.says: A pool chooses a member once per request and never moves it, so a null from the pool is an unknown outcome to reverse; a retry through the pool lands on another link as a second purchase.
basis: section:14.2 A Pool Chooses a Link Once per Request

aspects.says: The 2.1.7 round-robin counter is an int that goes negative after 2^31 increments, and from then on every request on the pool throws.
basis: section:14.4.1 Spot the Problem: Eight Months of Uptime
aspects.reason: the wrap needs 2^31 requests or reflection into the pool's private counter; the lesson shows the run, and the router practice uses a floor modulo without testing a wrap

aspects.says: When host instances do not share state, a follow-up must go to its original's link, found through field 41 and field 90, and wait while that link is down; the override strategy falls back to round-robin instead, so it needs a router of your own.
basis: section:14.6 A Follow-Up That Must Reach Its Original's Host Needs a Router of Your Own

aspects.says: With nothing usable the pool polls once a second inside the request's own budget and returns null with nothing sent, so the caller checks isConnected first.
basis: section:14.5 With Nothing Usable, the Pool Spends the Request's Own Time

aspects.says: primary-secondary fails back at once, round-robin spreads a dead member's share evenly by advancing its counter per skipped member, and split-by-divisor falls back to round-robin when its member is down.
basis: section:14.4 The Strategy Decides Where Traffic Goes When a Link Fails

aspects.says: With check-enabled a member is usable only while its enabled mark is the very ready object of its current connection; without it a connected member is usable.
basis: section:14.3 A Link Is Usable When It Is Connected and Signed On

aspects.says: request(m, 0) on a 2.1.7 pool sends the message and then hands it to a member again.
basis: section:14.5 With Nothing Usable, the Pool Spends the Request's Own Time
aspects.reason: it depends on two calls landing in the same millisecond, which a deterministic test cannot arrange; the lesson shows the run
